The Garden of Earthly Delights. Hieronymus Bosch's monumental triptych, painted around 1490 to 1510, presents a fantastical panorama of paradise, earthly pleasures, and infernal punishment spread across three hinged panels. When fully opened, this oak painting measures about 2.2 metres high by 3.9 metres wide, and every inch is packed with meticulous detail and vivid colour that demands attention.

The left panel shows the Garden of Eden with the creation of Eve and all manner of mysterious hybrid creatures. The centre panel—the garden of earthly delights itself—swarms with naked figures engaged in sensual pleasures, feasting, courtship, and play among impossible architecture and giant fruits. The right panel shows Hell, a terrifying landscape of torture, fire, and punishment ruled by a hybrid demon-figure seated on a throne.

The painting has hung in the Prado Museum in Madrid since the eighteenth century, but its true meaning remains debated among scholars even now. Bosch's intricate weaving of flora, fauna, and human forms influenced the Surrealist artists of the twentieth century, cementing his visionary style as the most celebrated work of his career and a defining moment of Northern Renaissance imagination.
